title: The Next School of War: Educating for Tomorrow's Battlefield
gist: Marine Corps University's president and a faculty chair describe reforms shifting professional military education toward a classified, all-domain curriculum built around battle labs, wargaming, and AI, arguing that traditional history-and-strategy-heavy schooling has not kept pace with multidomain warfare against China, Russia, and Iran.

themes.theme: Military education is out of step with modern warfare

insights.claim: Professional military education still emphasizes classical history and strategy seminars disconnected from the technical realities of AI-enabled, multidomain modern warfare.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Frames a structural gap between officer training and the technical/AI-driven battlefield they will actually fight on.
insights.quote: Professional military education tends to reinforce stale seminars and lectures that reflect concerns about strategy and history disconnected from the technical reality of modern warfare.
insights.locator: Yet, military education has not kept up

insights.claim: Historically, major shifts in the character of war have forced corresponding reforms in military schooling, from Scharnhorst's reforms after Napoleonic warfare to Breckinridge's 1929 call for pragmatist, experiential learning in the interwar Marine Corps.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Establishes a historical pattern the authors use to justify the current reform push as timely rather than fashionable.
insights.quote: In 1929, James Carson Breckinridge, a Marine officer, published “Some Thoughts on Service Schools” in the Marine Corps Gazette, calling for a new educational paradigm consistent with John Dewey’s ideas about pragmatism and experiential learning.

insights.claim: Despite months of US and Israeli bombing and intermittent clashes, Iran retains the ability to launch drone, missile, and cyber attacks, which the authors say should be a clarion call about the difficulty of breaking modern anti-access networks.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Real-world evidence that even sustained strike campaigns are not degrading adversary anti-access/area-denial capability as quickly as expected.
insights.quote: The fact that after months of bombing and intermittent clashes, Iran retains the ability to launch drone, missile, and cyber attacks, should be a clarion call.
insights.locator: This technical requirement is driven by the challenge

insights.claim: China presents an anti-access and area-denial challenge an order of magnitude larger than Russia or Iran, given its deeper space, cyber, and long-strike capabilities.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Sets China as the pacing threat driving the curriculum redesign, above Russia/Ukraine and Iran scenarios.
insights.quote: China presents an order of magnitude larger challenge with deeper space, cyber, and long-strike capabilities.

themes.theme: Marine Corps University's classified curriculum overhaul

insights.claim: Marine Corps University built a pilot Joint All-Domain Operations curriculum at the top-secret/sensitive compartmented information level, centered on the Command and Staff College under faculty leads Nathan Packard and Joseph McAlarnen.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of a US service moving officer education into classified spaces to close the theory-practice gap.
insights.quote: We started by building a pilot curriculum for Joint All-Domain Operations at the top-secret and sensitive compartmented information level.

insights.claim: By graduation, an Intermediate Level School major must be able to coordinate distinct advantages across multiple domains to fight a single Joint Task Force at the echelon II level, such as Pacific Fleet or Marine Forces Pacific.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Defines a concrete, measurable proficiency bar the new curriculum is designed to hit.
insights.quote: the Intermediate Level School graduate must possess the skills to effectively fight a single Joint Task Force at the echelon II level (e.g., Pacific Fleet, Marine Forces Pacific).
insights.locator: By graduation from Intermediate Level School

insights.claim: The authors argue that expecting officers to master modern warfare using only unclassified materials is like teaching surgery to medical students barred from cutting on cadavers.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Justifies pushing the bulk of technical military education into classified settings as a practical necessity, not a preference.
insights.quote: expecting officers to master modern warfare using exclusively unclassified materials resembles teaching surgery to medical students restricted from cutting on cadavers.
insights.locator: As a result, expecting officers to master modern warfare

insights.claim: Faculty development now sends historians to space camp to learn orbital mechanics and political scientists to study command and control and joint fires, pairing academic instructors with fleet exercises and joint staffs.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Shows the reform extends beyond the syllabus into how faculty themselves are trained and certified.
insights.quote: Our historians now attend space camp to understand orbital mechanics. Political scientists study command and control and joint fires.
insights.locator: Transforming the curriculum also required a new approach

insights.claim: The Gray Scholars program at the Command and Staff College has students support real initiatives such as the future of urban warfare and DARPA's mosaic warfare concept, developing individual research tied to classified wargames.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: An existing model for embedding students directly in live defense research and planning problems, now being scaled university-wide.
insights.quote: This program saw students support efforts ranging from thinking about the future of urban warfare to force design and the Defense Advanced Research Project Agency’s mosaic warfare.
insights.locator: Much of it started with the Gray Scholars program

insights.claim: Since the Brute Krulak Center formed in 2016, Marine Corps University has run an annual head-to-head wargaming competition called Sea Dragon (started 2018), a model since replicated by the international Fight Club Society.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Documents an eight-year track record of institutionalized wargaming that the new reforms are now expanding into classified formats.
insights.quote: Starting in 2018, the program used an annual competition, Sea Dragon, to pit students in head-to-head fights in modern scenarios.
insights.locator: Since the formation of the Brute Krulak Center

insights.claim: Marine Corps University's AI integration began in 2018 with Project Athena, using wargame tournaments to generate human data later converted into machine courses of action, later extended via DARPA STORM models and genetic algorithms.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Traces an eight-year institutional history of AI-for-planning experimentation predating the current LLM wave.
insights.quote: It started in 2018 with Project Athena and using wargame tournaments to generate human data that could be turned into machine courses of action.

insights.claim: The authors warn that AI is a general-purpose technology that must be adapted to the fog and friction of war, cautioning that 'stochastic parroting is not a method' for military decision-making.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: A explicit caution against over-trusting generative AI outputs in operational planning, relevant to how militaries and vendors should scope AI decision-support tools.
insights.quote: The fact is, AI is a general-purpose technology that must be adapted to the fog and friction inherent in warfare. Just like hope, stochastic parroting is not a method.
insights.locator: The effort evolved as large language models

insights.claim: The authors argue tactics and military theory, civil-military relations and professional ethics, and military history/strategy/international relations remain foundational and must be preserved even as classified technical training expands.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Signals the reform is additive rather than a wholesale replacement of traditional strategic education, relevant to how other war colleges might calibrate similar changes.
insights.quote: Preparing officers for the realities of multidomain combat against peer adversaries requires reforming but not fundamentally breaking or replacing professional military education.

insights.claim: The next phase of reform will extend classified, all-domain education to students at distance-education locations on major bases via secure facilities (SCIFs) and a new blended seminar program.
insights.speaker: Brig. Gen. Matthew Tracy and Benjamin Jensen
insights.so_what: Indicates the classified-curriculum model is intended to scale beyond the pilot cohort to the broader officer corps.
insights.quote: Marine Corps Distance Education and Training has introduced a blended seminar program that teaches all domain war at the classified level.
